kp.k: SuperLawyer targets routine and sophisticated attorney tasks
kp.d: The July 9, 2024 article describes SuperLawyer as a subscription-based generative AI chatbot assisting attorneys with document review, summaries, legal research and drafting. It positions the platform as supporting lawyers rather than replacing them, with more time for higher-value human work presented as an expected benefit, not a measured outcome.
qs: It is a subscription-based AI chatbot that assists attorneys with routine and sophisticated legal tasks, such as document reviews, summaries, legal research and document drafting.
By freeing lawyers from such time-consuming work, the AI-powered legal service is expected to help legal professionals focus more on higher-value, human work like building client relationships.

kp.k: Paid access is restricted to licensed lawyers
kp.d: The article calls SuperLawyer Korea’s first paid AI legal assistant platform, while reporting that local competitors are developing similar services. Following an initial free period, payment is required starting in August 2024, and access is limited to licensed lawyers. The article compares its services to Casetext’s CoCounsel.
qs: Local legal tech companies have rushed to develop similar AI legal assistant services but SuperLawyer is Korea’s first paid AI legal assistant platform.
Starting in August, users must pay to access it, and only licensed lawyers can use it.
It offers similar services to those provided by California-based legal AI company Casetext’s legal service, CoCounsel.

kp.k: Local legal database supports the platform's training
kp.d: The article reports that SuperLawyer is trained with Law&Company’s Bigcase database, described as containing about 4.6 million local precedents and legal content. It also reports 1,230 registered members during nine days of free service following launch earlier that month; this is registration evidence rather than evidence of paid adoption or task performance.
qs: SuperLawyer is trained with Law&Copmany’s Bigcase, a database boasting about 4.6 million local precedents and legal content.
Since its official launch earlier this month, its free service has garnered 1,230 registered members in nine days.

kp.k: Attorney assistance is positioned to avoid professional conflict
kp.d: The article contrasts SuperLawyer with LawTalk, which connects users to lawyers and charges lawyers for advertising. It reports that the Korean Bar Association has challenged LawTalk since 2015 over alleged encroachment on the profession. Communications director Um Boun expects no similar conflict over SuperLawyer because it improves attorneys’ efficiency and asserts that the company has confirmed regulatory compliance; these are company positions, not reported regulatory determinations.
qs: It has launched legal challenges against Law&Company’s services since the release of LawTalk in 2015.

But the startup does not expect any similar conflict with the KBA over SuperLawyer because the new platform is designed to improve efficiency in attorneys’ work, said Um Boun, communications director at Law&Company.
“We have confirmed that it (SuperLawyer) does not violate any ordinance,” added Um.

kp.k: Company plans US expansion within five years
kp.d: Founder and CEO Kim Bon-hwan presents SuperLawyer as a vehicle for entering the US legal technology market within five years of the 2024 report. His stated ambition includes representing Korea at the American Bar Association’s ABA TECHSHOW. This is a prospective expansion plan rather than evidence of an existing US presence.
qs: Law&Company Co., the operator of South Korea’s largest legal advice app LawTalk, will venture into the US legal tech market in five years with its new service SuperLawyer, Korea’s first-ever artificial intelligence-powered legal assistant platform, its founder said on Thursday.

“It is expected to open a new era for Korea’s legal services, and we will represent Korea at the ABA TECHSHOW organized by the American Bar Association in the US, home to legal tech, with our services in five years.”

kp.k: Market forecast anticipates substantial legal AI growth
kp.d: The article cites Business Research Insights for a forecast that the global legal tech AI market will grow from $8.1 billion in 2021 to $46.5 billion in 2027. This is a reported market projection, not an observed growth result.
qs: The global legal tech AI market is expected to grow to $46.5 billion in 2027 from $8.1 billion in 2021, according to Business Research Insights.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: SuperLawyer is presented as augmenting lawyers by performing legal tasks and freeing time for higher-value human work.
pts.d: Eun-Yi Ko describes SuperLawyer as a subscription chatbot assisting with document review, summaries, legal research and drafting, including both routine and sophisticated tasks. The article predicts that this assistance will let lawyers concentrate more on client relationships. CEO Kim Bon-hwan presents the product as a reliable partner that will help Korean legal professionals adopt AI. This is an augmentation claim, not a claim that the product will replace lawyers; no specific human verification process is described.

pts.k: Law&Company forecasts domestic legal-service transformation and plans entry into the US legal-tech market within five years.
pts.d: Kim predicts that SuperLawyer will open a new era for Korean legal services and says the company will represent Korea at ABA TECHSHOW in five years. Ko characterizes this ambition as venturing into the US legal-tech market. The article also identifies SuperLawyer as Korea's first paid AI legal assistant platform and reports competing development efforts by local legal-tech companies. These are software-market claims about a legal-tech vendor, not claims about an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work.

pts.k: Law&Company expects its lawyer-assistance model to avoid the professional conflict experienced by LawTalk.
pts.d: Communications director Um Boun says the company does not expect a similar conflict with the Korean Bar Association over SuperLawyer because it improves attorneys' efficiency. Um also asserts that the company has confirmed the platform violates no ordinance. The article contrasts this positioning with the association's challenges to LawTalk over alleged encroachment on the legal profession. The anticipated absence of conflict and the compliance assertion are attributed to the company, not to a regulator or court.

pts.k: The article reports a forecast of substantial global legal-tech AI market growth.
pts.d: Ko reports, citing Business Research Insights, that the global legal-tech AI market is expected to reach $46.5 billion in 2027, compared with $8.1 billion in 2021. This is a market-size forecast rather than an observed outcome or a prediction specifically about SuperLawyer's revenue.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article offers product descriptions, training-data scale and initial registrations, but no measured productivity or reliability results.
pts.d: Ko reports that SuperLawyer was trained with the company's Bigcase database of about 4.6 million local precedents and legal content, and that its initially free service attracted 1,230 registered members in nine days. These provide development and early-adoption context; they are not reported as tests of accuracy, time savings, reliability or willingness to pay. The article compares the service offering to Casetext's CoCounsel without presenting a comparative benchmark. The transformation, reliability and international-expansion claims rest on Kim's statements. The conflict and compliance claims rest on Um's statements, with no legal opinion or regulatory ruling supplied. The market forecast is attributed to Business Research Insights without its methodology being reproduced.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The launch and adoption claims concern July 2024; paid access begins in August, international expansion is a five-year ambition, and the market forecast ends in 2027.
pts.d: In the July 9, 2024 article, SuperLawyer is described as having launched earlier that month, with registrations measured over nine days. Paid access is scheduled for August 2024, and use is restricted to licensed lawyers. Kim's five-year US ambition implies approximately 2029. No quantified deadline is given for productivity improvements or domestic transformation. Avoiding bar-association conflict is expressly linked to the product's attorney-efficiency purpose. The global market forecast uses 2021 as its baseline and 2027 as its endpoint.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Licensed Korean lawyers are the direct intended beneficiaries, while clients, professional bodies and legal-tech businesses are affected indirectly.
pts.d: Lawyers are expected to receive task assistance and gain time for client-facing work, while paying subscription fees after the introductory free period. Clients are positioned as indirect beneficiaries of greater attention to relationships; SuperLawyer is not described as a direct public-access legal advice service. Law&Company seeks domestic leadership and US expansion, while other Korean legal-tech companies are developing competing assistants. The Korean Bar Association is relevant to the company's expectation of reduced professional conflict. The article does not predict staffing reductions, distinguish firm sizes or lawyer seniority, or quantify client cost savings or access-to-justice effects.
